title: The Relationship Between Education and Adult Mortality in the United States
research_question: Does additional schooling causally reduce adult mortality, or is the well-documented negative correlation between education and health driven by confounding factors such as ability, parental background, time preferences, or reverse causality from childhood health to schooling? If a causal effect exists, how large is it relative to conventional correlational estimates?
data_description: The study uses 1% random samples from the 1960, 1970, and 1980 U.S. Censuses (IPUMS) to construct synthetic cohorts of white individuals born in the 48 contiguous states who were 14 years old between 1914 and 1939. Observations are aggregated by gender, single-year birth cohort, and state of birth, yielding roughly 4,795 cells with two ten-year mortality rates per cell (1960–70 and 1970–80) computed from changes in cell population counts. Key variables include completed years of education, gender, age, and state-of-birth characteristics measured when the individual was 14 (percent urban, percent foreign-born, percent black, manufacturing employment and wages, farm value per acre, doctors per capita, education expenditures per capita, school buildings per square mile). Individual-level mortality results are validated using the NHANES I Epidemiologic Follow-up Study (NHEFS), which tracks 4,554 whites through 1985. State-level compulsory attendance and child labor laws (entry age, work-permit age, continuation-school requirements) for 1915–1939 are matched to each cohort.
institutional_context: Between 1915 and 1939, U.S. secondary schooling expanded dramatically, with the share of young adults holding high-school diplomas rising from about 9% in 1910 to over 50% by 1940. During this window, at least 30 states repeatedly amended their compulsory school attendance laws and child labor laws, altering the minimum age at which children had to enter school, the age at which they could obtain work permits and leave school, and whether working children had to attend continuation schools part-time. These statutes were uncoordinated across the two domains and varied substantially across states and over time, with some states tightening requirements and others briefly loosening them. Unlike earlier decades when such laws were widely viewed as unenforceable, contemporaneous and historical evidence indicates the laws were meaningfully enforced from the 1920s onward, before declining in relevance after the 1940s. This setting created cohort- and state-specific variation in mandated schooling that plausibly affected educational attainment without operating through other channels (e.g., school lunch programs) directly tied to health.
